column4: The question whether a human being may have whatever he wishes states the mistaken claim to choice that 53:25 answers by assigning both the later and the first to God.
After 10:48 demands the promised event, this ayah says every community has a term which it can neither delay nor advance by an hour.
No community can precede its appointed term or postpone it, repeating the exact advance-and-delay boundary developed by the section.
The demand to know when the promise will come supplies the impatient question answered by the fixed appointment in 34:30.
The promised appointment is a day from which people can neither delay nor advance by an hour, making the postponed event exact rather than indefinite.
At the arrival of punishment, wrongdoers ask to be postponed to a near term; the request exposes the point at which a desired extension is no longer available.
Those who demand punishment be hastened are told that an appointed term already governs it and that it will come suddenly.
God progressively draws deniers toward their end from where they do not know, supplying the movement whose apparent respite is named in 7:183.
God grants respite while His plan is firm, so temporal extension conceals rather than cancels the secured adverse outcome.
Deniers are progressively drawn from where they do not know before 68:45 names their respite, distinguishing delay from escape.
God fulfilled His promise to earlier messengers and saved them, presenting the later realization after the earlier word.
The people of Paradise say that God fulfilled His promise and gave them the land to inherit, showing the promised gift at receipt.
Those raised from their graves recognize the event as what the Merciful promised and the messengers truthfully announced.
When believers see the confederates, they identify the sight as the promise of God and His Messenger come true.
Another favor the believers love is announced as divine help and a near victory, marking a further gift that follows the one already named.
Whether the Prophet is shown part of what is promised or dies first, the people still return to God; fulfillment is not confined to the addressee's first-life horizon.
Whether the Prophet sees part of the promised outcome or dies before it, his task is delivery and God's is reckoning.
The command to be patient because God's promise is true is followed by the same boundary: its realization may be shown now or lie beyond the Prophet's death.
Even if God takes the Prophet away, vengeance on the deniers remains secured; 43:42 supplies the alternative of showing him the promise.
The alternative is that the Prophet is shown what the deniers were promised, and God's power over them guarantees either temporal route.
Israel's covenant includes lending God a good loan followed by expiation and entry into gardens, another present advance with secured later payment.
Men and women who lend God a good loan receive multiplication and a noble reward, repeating the section's deferred-transaction image.
A good loan to God is multiplied and forgiven, framing later divine increase as repayment of a present advance.
A person's striving will later be seen, so work done in the first interval remains held for disclosure.
The striving shown in 53:40 is then repaid with the fullest recompense, completing the deferred-payment sequence.
The garden owners make no reservation when fixing their morning harvest, intensifying the false certainty reversed during the night.
At morning the owners call one another, marking the appointed harvest time after the unseen nocturnal loss.
They set out early to cut the crop if they truly intend to harvest, continuing the expected act whose failure is disclosed in 68:26–27.
The believing companion says his Lord may give him a garden better than the other's and send ruin on the present garden, opposing warranted hope to boastful certainty.
The command to look at fruit when it first bears and when it ripens makes the interval between beginning and completed yield visible.
The later garden's fruit is neither cut off nor forbidden, turning the section's fruit preserved to harvest into provision without an ending.
The king's vision of seven cows and seven ears is the image whose interpretation in 12:47–49 unfolds as a long scheduled sequence of harvest, storage, scarcity, and relief.
Everything upon the earth passes away, stating the vanishing side of the temporal scale completed by what remains in 55:27.
The face of the Lord remains after all earthly beings pass, giving the abiding counterpart to 55:26.
Everything perishes except God, judgment belongs to Him, and all return to Him; passing possession and final destination meet in one ayah.
Flood foam disappears while what benefits people remains in the earth, a concrete Quranic measure of transient appearance against lasting good.
Worldly ornament is called mere enjoyment while the afterlife with the Lord belongs to the Godfearing.
Worldly life is only a brief enjoyment when measured against the afterlife, repeating the scale used in 4:77.
The unbelievers' movement through the land is only a little enjoyment before their adverse lodging; 3:198 gives the opposite later hospitality.
The Godfearing receive abiding gardens as hospitality from God, and what is with Him is better for the righteous.
The punishment of the afterlife is more severe and more enduring, a direct reversal in which later is greater and lasting but not better for its recipient.
Those who withhold God's bounty think the withholding good for them, but its later embodiment as a collar exposes their mistaken comparison.
The ayah asks whether the threatened fate is better or the eternal garden promised to the Godfearing, explicitly choosing between two eventual outcomes.
The question whether one cast into the Fire is better than one arriving safe on Resurrection Day makes the final result decide between two cases.
Some fighters wanted this world and others wanted the afterlife, locating the two temporal choices inside one event and its immediate spoils.
After creation, some people are returned to a frail age and lose former knowledge; a person's own later phase can therefore diminish rather than improve.
After successive embryonic stages God brings the human being forth as another creation, establishing the first life before 23:15–16's death and resurrection.
After that created life human beings will die, the boundary between the first creation of 23:14 and the raising in 23:16.
After death people will be raised on Resurrection Day, completing the ordered first-life and second-life sequence.
The ayah orders nonlife, first life, death, renewed life, and return to God, staging an entire succession whose later creation supplies the destination.
The condemned acknowledge two deaths and two lives, directly distinguishing repeated life stages when the final outcome has become visible.
At judgment a person wishes he had sent something ahead for his true life, naming the later existence as the life for which the first should have prepared.
The warning addresses whoever wishes to advance or lag behind, using the same opposition between preceding and coming later that defines الآخر in the section.
Deniers claim there is only the first death and no raising, explicitly rejecting the second creation denoted by the later abode.
The question whether God tired at the first creation exposes confusion about a new creation, pairing the first beginning with the disputed later one.
God begins and repeats creation, a compact formulation of the first origin followed by renewed creation.
The One who begins creation and then repeats it also provides from heaven and earth, joining second creation to continuing provision.
God begins creation, repeats it, and then people return to Him, ordering origin, second creation, and destination.
God begins creation and repeats it, and the repeated creation is easier for Him, reinforcing the certainty of the later arising.
The One who originated bones the first time will give them life again, making the first creation evidence for the later one.
The people of Paradise say the messengers brought the truth as they are told to inherit the garden, a promised later home recognized at arrival.
People see the promised punishment as far away, stating the human perception of delay that 70:7 reverses.
God sees the supposedly distant event as near, exposing the difference between perceived postponement and its true divine measure.
What people are promised is declared true, preserving certainty before 51:6 identifies the coming judgment.
Judgment is certain to occur, supplying the adverse event guaranteed by the promise of 51:5.
What the hearers are promised will certainly occur, a bare assurance whose content is judgment rather than gift.
Deniers ask when the promise will come, the impatient challenge that ends with their recognition after rising in 36:52.
The trumpet is blown and people rush from the graves, staging the arrival immediately before 36:52 identifies it as the old promise.
Iblis asks to be postponed until Resurrection Day so he can master Adam's descendants; the same delay form serves a hostile project rather than a secured good.
Usurious increase does not grow with God, while almsgiving is multiplied, distinguishing apparent present gain from true eventual increase.
The parable begins with vineyards surrounded by date palms, supplying the fruit-bearing scene whose presumed permanence and collapse appear in 18:36–42.
Abundant fruit names the provision whose decisive lasting property, being neither cut off nor forbidden, is stated in 56:33.
The command to glorify God in evening and morning marks two stages of the daily sequence continued in 30:18.
Praise at late day and noon completes the ordered day begun in 30:17, paralleling the section's attention to a named daylight threshold.
Prayer at the two ends of day and early night maps worship onto temporal boundaries rather than a single undifferentiated day.
The moon follows the sun, adding succession to the solar-brightness oath of 91:1.
The day reveals the sun, further defining the illumination staged by the ضُحَىٰ oath in 91:1.
The catalogue of immediate human desires ends by locating the good destination with God, moving evaluation from present attraction to final return.
At Joseph's establishment in Egypt, God says He will teach him taʾwīl and will prevail in His affair, an early stage whose distant result appears in 12:100.
After the dream's fulfillment Joseph recalls being taught taʾwīl and asks to be joined with the righteous, placing interpretation within his life's reached outcome.
God creates death and life to test which people are best in deed, joining life's endpoints to a divine comparison of what is better.
A former people are made predecessors and an example for later peoples, using earlier and later generations as a moral sequence.
The blessed speakers say they will suffer only their first death and no punishment, making that first death the passed boundary of their lasting later condition.
Believers ask God to give what He promised through His messengers and not disgrace them on the later Day, voicing reliance on deferred assurance.
At the point when believers ask when divine help will come, the answer says God's help is near, a concise response to felt delay.
The Prophet is directed to night worship in hope that his Lord will raise him to a praised station, a personally addressed better state still ahead.
Promised gardens are followed by God's greater pleasure, so even the named later gift opens onto something described as greater.
The satisfied soul is commanded to return to its Lord, joining attained رضا to the final place of return.
The Messenger says he does not know whether the promised event is near or whether his Lord has assigned it a long term, explicitly separating certainty from timing.
After clear warning, the Messenger says he does not know whether the promised event is near or far, preserving the promise while withholding its schedule.
